Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

issues.item: Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the trigger set is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile: darkness and especially tactile/unexpected touch are more characteristic of direct interpersonal assault than of a loved-one trauma, and there is no accompanying memory or appraisal content that links touch or darkness to this trauma.

The lock-checking threat item and parallel checking-locks strategy suggest a home-intrusion or direct personal danger formulation. In a loved-one trauma profile, this can occur, but here it is not supported by any appraisals or memory content about preventing another loss, danger to family, or responsibility. As selected, these items pull toward a different trauma narrative than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Within the allowed nodes, the strongest coherence is around hyperarousal and intrusive memory, but the specific combination of tactile triggers plus lock-checking behavior is difficult to explain as one coherent formulation for a loved-one trauma without any linked negative appraisal content. This is more than merely unusual because the selected items imply different threat contexts.

The trigger/threat pattern is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of trauma to a loved one. Tactile unexpected-touch triggers plus broad startle to nearby movement are more typical of direct assault or personal threat trauma, not bereavement-focused trauma, unless there is additional context not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Door/lock checking and hypervigilant startle responses imply an ongoing fear of intruders or immediate physical attack, but the rest of the profile centers on intrusive memory and loss-related trigger content rather than a coherent physical-danger narrative tied to the loved-one trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, Threat is strongly linked to Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies, but the selected threat items reflect personal safety/intruder danger whereas the only clearly trauma-congruent trigger is loss-themed conversation. This creates a poor match between the active nodes: the threat content does not plausibly arise from the listed trauma-relevant triggers.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, tactile triggering by unexpected touch is not impossible, but paired with the rest of this profile it implies a direct personal-assault or physical-threat theme that is not supported by the memory items or the loss-focused trigger item. This makes the trigger set clinically incoherent around the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Repeated door/window lock checking suggests an ongoing home-intrusion or personal safety threat appraisal. In a profile centered on trauma to a loved one, with memory items focused on reliving and no appraisals linking the event to current intruder danger, this threat item does not fit the dominant loss-based formulation and appears mismatched with the other selected items.

issues.item: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeatedly checking locks/doors/windows is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and the indexed trauma type (trauma to a loved one). The other selected items center on grief/loss reminders, intrusive vivid replay, and generalized startle, but do not indicate a home-intrusion, assault, or safety-compulsion theme that would make lock-checking a coherent trauma-linked strategy. As selected, this item appears to target a threat-management pattern not otherwise represented in triggers, memory, or appraisals.

vignette:
James Chen was forty-eight when he walked into the therapist's office, though he looked older—the kind of worn that comes not from years but from months of living sideways through them. He owned a hardware store in Portland, Oregon, one his father had started thirty years ago, and until last year he had been the kind of man who greeted customers by name, who knew the difference between a Phillips and a Robertson head, who took pride in keeping the shelves straight and the register honest. That man had begun to disappear on a Tuesday in September when his younger brother Michael called from Seattle with a voice James had never heard before, a voice that was not quite his brother's voice anymore.

Michael had been hit by a delivery truck while crossing the street. He was thirty-eight. He died in the ambulance. James had not been there—had only heard the description from his sister, who had received the call from the hospital—but the image had constructed itself in his mind with the precision of lived memory. The truck's grille approaching Michael's body. The sound of impact, which James had never actually heard but which his brain had manufactured so completely that he could no longer distinguish it from something he had witnessed. The awful finality. In the weeks immediately after, James had functioned in a kind of anesthetized shock. He attended the funeral and stood beside his mother while she wept, held his sister's hand, listened to people talk about Michael's kindness, his humor, his two young children. The casket was closed. James was grateful for that. But he was also certain, with a certainty that felt absolute, that if he allowed himself to think about what was inside that box, what remained of his brother after being struck by two tons of metal, he would not survive it. So he had simply decided not to think about it. He stopped attending family dinners. He made excuses when his sister called. When his wife, Patricia, tried to talk about Michael or suggest they visit his grave to plant flowers on his birthday, James would leave the room and light a cigarette on the back porch, standing in the cold until Patricia gave up and closed the door.

The problem was that the decision not to think about Michael had become impossible to maintain. The memory came anyway, uninvited and complete. James would be restocking shelves and suddenly he was there—not remembering it, but *in* it, watching the truck's grille approaching Michael's body, hearing the sound, feeling the impact as if his own ribs were breaking. The memory was not something that had happened; it was something that *was happening*, moment by moment, as vivid and immediate as if he were living it in real time. And then it would loop. Again. The truck. The moment of contact. The awful finality. Again. Again. And again. Three months after the funeral, James noticed he was jumping at sounds in the store. A customer dropped a can of paint and James flinched so violently he knocked a display of hinges onto the floor. His hands were shaking. He told the customer he was sorry, that he hadn't slept well, which was true—he had been smoking more, sometimes going through a pack a day, and staying up late watching television with the volume loud enough to drown out his own thoughts. When the bell above the door chimed—the same bell that had hung there for thirty years—James felt a spike of something between fear and rage, as if the sound itself were a threat. Unexpected movement in his peripheral vision sent him into a state of raw alertness, his body tensing as if danger were genuinely present. The feeling would linger for minutes after the trigger passed, his heart still racing, his muscles still coiled. He knew, rationally, that a customer browsing the electrical section was not a threat. But his body did not know this. His body believed he was in constant danger.

By spring, James had begun avoiding anything that might trigger the memory or the feelings it brought. He stopped listening to the radio because songs could remind him of Michael. He asked Patricia not to talk about loss, about grief, about people who had died—which meant he asked her not to talk about most of what was happening in their family, because his mother was struggling, his sister was struggling, and there were few conversations anymore that did not circle back to absence. Patricia had stopped trying. She had stopped asking him to go anywhere that might involve seeing people, because she had learned that his anger and his startle responses made those outings difficult. The store was becoming harder too. Customers would sometimes mention their own losses—a father, a friend—and James would feel his chest tighten, would excuse himself to the back room, would smoke another cigarette and wait until the customer left. What frightened him most was not just the memory itself, though it had grown more intrusive, more vivid, more present with each passing month. It was the thought that the world had become fundamentally unsafe, that sudden, random violence could take anyone at any time, and that there was no way to predict or prevent it. Michael had been crossing the street. Michael had been doing something ordinary. And now Michael was gone. This knowledge sat underneath everything James did now—a baseline assumption that danger was constant, that vigilance was the only thing standing between him and another loss.

What finally brought James to therapy was not the memory itself but his daughter calling from college to say she was worried about him, that her mother had told her he seemed unreachable, that he had missed her birthday dinner. It was the realization that in trying not to think about Michael, in trying not to feel the horror and the guilt and the anger, he had begun to lose Patricia too, and his daughter, and the version of himself that had once owned a hardware store with genuine pleasure. He was afraid—deeply, constantly afraid—that if he stopped running from the memory, if he stopped smoking and avoiding and turning away, he would be swallowed by it entirely. But he was also afraid, perhaps more afraid, that the life he was living now was already a kind of death, and that Michael's death had somehow killed him too. At forty-eight, James sat in the therapist's office knowing only that something had to change, though the thought of change itself—of facing what he had been running from—felt like stepping directly into the path of that truck all over again.
